'''''Bellardia trixago''''' is a [[species]] of flowering plant in the family [[Orobanchaceae]]. It was formerly classified in the family [[Scrophulariaceae]]. The only member of the [[Monotypic taxon|monotypic]] genus '''''Bellardia''''', it is known as '''trixago bartsia'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''Mediterranean lineseed'''.<ref>{{Cite PLANTS|id=BETR|taxon=Bellardia trixago|access-date=9 January 2016}}</ref> This plant is native to the [[Mediterranean Basin]], but it is known in other places with similar climates, such as [[California]] and parts of [[Chile]], where it is an [[introduced species]] and [[noxious weed]].{{not verified in body|date=October 2024}}

== Description ==
{{no citations section|date=October 2024}}
''Bellardia trixago'' is an erect plant often reaching over half a meter in height. Its foliage is rich green and dotted with glands and hairs. The sawtoothed leaves extend about halfway up the plant, with the upper half of the stem being occupied with a stout [[inflorescence]] which narrows to a point. The inflorescence has rows of leaflike [[bract]]s, between which emerge showy purple and white lipped, hooded flowers, each over two centimeters wide. The fruit is a smooth, green capsule. Mediterranean lineseed, like other broomrapes, is [[Parasitic plant|parasitic]]; this species is hemiparasitic in that it is green and photosynthetic but also taps into the roots of other plants to extract nutrients.

== Phylogeny ==
The phylogeny of the genera of [[Rhinantheae]] has been explored using molecular characters.<ref name="Tesitel2010"/><ref name="Scheunert2012"/> ''Bellardia'' belongs to the core Rhinantheae. ''Bellardia'' is closely related to ''[[Parentucellia]]'', to some ''[[Bartsia]]'' taxa, and to ''[[Odontites]]''.<ref name="Scheunert2012" /><ref name="UribeConvers2016">{{Cite journal |last1=Uribe-Convers |first1=Simon |last2=Tank |first2=David C. |date=2016-09-01 |title=Phylogenetic revision of the genus ''Bartsia'' (Orobanchaceae): disjunct distributions correlate to independent lineages |url=http://openurl.ingenta.com/content/xref?genre=article&issn=0363-6445&volume=41&issue=3&spage=672 |journal=Systematic Botany |language=en |volume=41 |issue=3 |pages=672–684 |doi=10.1600/036364416x692299 |s2cid=88752480 |issn=0363-6445|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In turn, these genera share phylogenetic affinities with ''[[Tozzia]]'' and ''[[Hedbergia]]'', and then with ''[[Euphrasia]]'' and ''[[Bartsia]]''.{{cn|date=October 2024}}

== Etymology ==
The genus name ''Bellardia'' is a [[Patronym (taxonomy)#Naming process|taxonomic patronym]] in honor of [[:it:Carlo Antonio Lodovico Bellardi|Carlo Antonio Lodovico Bellardi]] (1741–1826), an Italian botanist from [[Piedmont]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Rameau |first1=Jean-Claude |last2=Mansion |first2=Dominique |last3=Dumé |first3=G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P282nNjQq50C&pg=PA1261 |title=Flore forestière française: guide écologique illustré. Région méditerranéenne |date=2008 |page=1261 |publisher=Forêt privée française |isbn=978-2-904740-93-0 |language=fr}}</ref>

The species name ''trixago'' has two possible etymologies.
* It derives from the [[Ancient Greek]] word {{wikt-lang|grc|θρίξ}} ({{grc-transl|θρίξ}}), meaning "hair",<ref name="Bailly1981">{{Cite book |title=Abrégé du dictionnaire grec français |last=Bailly |first=Anatole |date=1981-01-01 |publisher=Hachette |isbn=978-2010035289 |location=Paris |oclc=461974285 }}</ref><ref name="Tabularium">{{Cite web |url=http://www.tabularium.be/bailly/ |title=Greek-french dictionary online |last=Bailly |first=Anatole |date= |website=www.tabularium.be |publisher= |access-date=May 2, 2020 |archive-date=March 18, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220318000653/http://www.tabularium.be/bailly/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> and the [[Latin]] suffix {{Lang|la|ago}}used to indicate a property, and refers to the glandular-hairy characteristic of the plant.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Page T |url=http://www.calflora.net/botanicalnames/pageT.html |website=www.calflora.net |access-date=2020-05-02 }}</ref><ref name="PlantMed">{{Cite web |title=''Bartsia'' |url=http://www.plante-mediterraneenne.fr/genres/bartsia/ |website=Plante Méditerranéenne |language=fr |access-date=2020-05-02 }}</ref>
* It derives from the Ancient Greek word {{wikt-lang|grc|τριξός}}, {{wikt-lang|grc|τρισσός}}, or {{wikt-lang|grc|τριττός}} ({{grc-transl|τριξός}}, {{grc-transl|τρισσός}}, or {{grc-transl|τριττός}}), meaning "triple",<ref name="Bailly1981" /><ref name="Tabularium" /> and refers to the trilobate lower lip of the flower.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gentil |first=Ambroise |year=1923 |title=Dictionnaire étymologique de la flore française |page=229 |publisher=Paul Lechevalier |place=Paris |url=http://fmbds.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Dictionnaire%20etymologique%20de%20la%20flore%20francaise%20Gentil%201923.pdf }}</ref> It is also the old Latin name of germanders (genus ''[[Teucrium]]'').<ref name="PlantMed" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
This plant is native to the Mediterranean Basin, but it is known in other places with similar climates, such as California and parts of Chile, where it is an introduced species and noxious weed.
